Welcome to Overview for AI Governance, part of the AI for Business Leaders online series for ISCA. I am Ray Han, Chief AI Trainer at HGT Consultancy. Over the next thirty minutes we will work out which rules actually apply to the AI your organisation is already running, who owns the risk, what to ask of any new proposal, and what to do about it in the next ninety days.

WHAT YOU ARE MISSING

Four things you still do not know.

Data

What data the chatbot collects and what it was trained on

Money

What it can tell a customer that costs you money

Customers

Where your customers are sitting when they use it

The framework is voluntary. The Personal Data Protection Act is not.
Need more information is the right answer. "No" is also reasonable. "Yes" is not. IMDA wrote the Model Framework, and says in the framework itself that adopting it "will not absolve organisations from compliance with current laws and regulations." The framework is voluntary. The Personal Data Protection Act is not. Four things you still do not know: what data the chatbot collects and what it was trained on; what it can tell a customer that costs you money; where your customers are sitting when they use it; and who in your organisation answers for it when it is wrong. Those four gaps are the next 28 minutes. None of them is answered by a framework, and all of them are answerable by you. If you picked Yes, you have company. In the Bank of England and FCA survey of UK financial firms, 46% of those using AI reported only partial understanding of the AI they use.

If you picked yes, you have company. In the Bank of England and FCA survey of UK financial firms, seventy-five per cent were already using AI, and forty-six per cent of those using it reported only partial understanding of the AI they use. The gap you just felt is the normal condition, not a personal failing. The rest of this course is the map.

FORTY-SEVEN COUNTRIES

The same definition of an AI system.

OECD, 2019
wrote it
2024
revised it
EU, Article 3(1)
almost word for word
Forty-seven countries have adhered to the same definition of an AI system. The OECD wrote it in 2019 and revised it in 2024. The EU copied it almost word for word into Article 3(1) of the AI Act. Agreement stops there.

WHERE AGREEMENT STOPS

One definition, many rulebooks.

The EU

risk tiers in law

Singapore and the UK

guidance rather than rules

India

binding rules on labelling synthetic content

Korea

a framework act

China

binding rules on generative AI and content labelling

The United States

litigating against its own states

The EU sets risk tiers in law, with fines reaching 7% of worldwide turnover. Singapore and the UK hand the job to the regulators that already exist, and publish guidance rather than rules. India says the same thing about philosophy, but has binding rules on labelling synthetic content in force since February 2026. Korea passed a framework act, in force January 2026. China has no comprehensive AI law, and binding rules on generative AI and content labelling that it already enforces. The United States reversed direction in 2025 and is now litigating against its own states.

THE QUESTION THAT HAS AN ANSWER

Ask a better question.

“Which of my uses, where, judged by whom?”

does have an answer

So "is AI regulated?" has no answer. The word covers a Korean statute, a Chinese labelling rule, a Singapore guideline and an American lawsuit against a state. "Which of my uses, where, judged by whom?" does have an answer, and you can work it out in an afternoon. That question is the shape of everything that follows.

THE THREE TIERS OF LEGAL FORCE

Three layers, all at once.

Binding law
Written for something else. Binds AI anyway.
Supervisory expectation
Not law. Not optional either.
Voluntary frameworks
Genuinely voluntary.
Every jurisdiction in this course has three layers, and all three apply to the same system at the same time. Binding law that was not written about AI, and binds anyway. Supervisory expectation — not law, not optional either. And voluntary frameworks, which are genuinely voluntary. The common mistake is reading these as a ranking, where satisfying the top one excuses the others. They are not a ranking, and satisfying one says nothing about the other two.

SINGAPORE FIRST

The same shape, twice.

Singapore United Kingdom
Binding law PDPA · Workplace Fairness Act · Online Criminal Harms Act codes UK GDPR & DPA 2018 · Equality Act · Online Safety Act
Supervisory expectation PDPC advisory guidelines · MAS guidelines ICO guidance · PRA SS1/23
Voluntary 3 Model AI Governance Frameworks · AI Verify AI Cyber Security Code · DSIT toolkit

Neither country has an AI Act.

Singapore stacks the three layers like this. Binding law that was never written about AI — the Personal Data Protection Act, the Workplace Fairness Act, the Online Criminal Harms Act codes. Supervisory expectation from the PDPC and MAS. And a thick voluntary layer: three Model AI Governance Frameworks and AI Verify. The United Kingdom arrives at the same shape by a different route, which is why it is worth one column. Neither country has an AI Act, and both have said why. Singapore: "We cannot adopt a one-size-fits-all approach to regulate it, nor can we anticipate every risk out there." The UK, from the despatch box in July 2026: "the best way of regulating is through context-specific regulation."

THE MIDDLE LAYER

“Non-binding” is not optional.

MAS, draft third-party risk management guidelines, March 2026

Where MAS is not satisfied with a firm's observance, it “may require the FI to take additional measures”, will “take non-observance into account in its assessment of the FI”, and “may also directly communicate with the home or host regulators of the FI and the FI's service provider.”

This is where executives misjudge, in both directions. Some treat guidance as law. Others treat it as decoration. MAS spelled out the cost of ignoring a non-binding guideline in its draft third-party risk management guidelines, published March 2026. Where MAS is not satisfied with a firm's observance, it may require the firm to take additional measures, will take non-observance into account in its assessment of the firm, and may also directly communicate with the home or host regulators of the firm and its service provider. Supervision enforces that guidance, rather than penalties. A firm that ignores it keeps its licence and loses the benefit of the doubt.

TWO DIMENSIONS

Legal force is not severity.

Legal force

Which layers apply to this use?

Consequence

How bad is it when this is wrong?

Tag the layers. Then rank by consequence. Separately.
Two dimensions, and mixing them is the most expensive error in this course. Legal force asks which layers apply. Consequence asks how bad it is when this is wrong. They are independent. A use can sit under binding law and be trivial. A use can sit under nothing but voluntary guidance and be the one that ends up in the newspaper. Adopting a framework does not move an activity into a low-risk bucket; it does not move it at all. So tag the layers, then rank by consequence, separately and in that order — the layers tell you who asks the questions, and the consequence tells you how fast you need an answer.

WHY THE EU REACHES YOU

The EU AI Act is partially live.

Postponed

High-risk obligations → Dec 2027 and Aug 2028
Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 Jul 2026

Already in force

Prohibitions — Feb 2025
General-purpose AI — Aug 2025
Article 50 transparency — Aug 2026

Penalties reach €35m or 7% of worldwide turnover, whichever is higher.
You are not in the EU. You may still be in scope. Article 2(1)(c) reaches providers and deployers in a third country where the output produced by the AI system is used in the Union. Some obligations were postponed: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July 2026, moved the high-risk obligations to December 2027 and August 2028. Others are already in force — prohibitions since February 2025, general-purpose AI obligations since August 2025, and Article 50 transparency since August 2026. Penalties reach 35 million euro, or 7% of worldwide turnover, whichever is higher.

CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING

Where is the exposure?

A Singapore retailer launches a chatbot that collects customer contact details and purchase history to personalise offers. The vendor follows the Model AI Governance Framework and displays an AI info card. The retailer has published nothing about how it uses customer data.

A
Covered. The Model Framework and the info card address transparency.

Both are voluntary. IMDA's own framework says adopting it “will not absolve organisations from compliance with current laws and regulations.”

B
The PDPA applies regardless, and voluntary measures do not discharge it.

The PDPA is binding law. PDPC's advisory guidelines interpret it. The Model Framework sits in a different tier and displaces neither.

C
Reputational only, since Singapore has no AI statute.

Singapore has no AI statute, and that changes nothing here. The PDPA binds whether or not AI is involved.

WHERE ENFORCEMENT ACTUALLY IS

What produced real consequences.

Dutch tax authority

2.75 million euros
At least 244,273 people were affected.

Australia's Robodebt scheme

1.763 billion Australian dollars of debt
roughly 433,000 people

Italy fined

Deliveroo 2.5 million euro
Glovo 5 million

All three turned on whether a person could argue with the decision.
The Dutch tax authority used nationality as an indicator in a risk-classification model. The regulator found that unlawful and discriminatory, and fined it 2.75 million euros. At least 244,273 people were affected. More than 43,000 are now recognised as victims, each receiving at least 30,000 euros. The cabinet resigned in January 2021. Australia's Robodebt scheme asserted 1.763 billion Australian dollars of debt against roughly 433,000 people. A judge called it "a massive failure of public administration." Italy fined Deliveroo 2.5 million euro and Glovo 5 million over rider-management algorithms, where a suspended rider "received an automatic message without any possibility of providing explanations or contesting the decision." None of these turned on how accurate the model was. All three turned on whether a person could argue with the decision.

THE HEADLINE AI FINES

The headline AI fines mostly did not survive.

OpenAI

Annulled

Italy fined Clearview AI

never collected

The UK fined Clearview

still unadjudicated on the merits

New York City's hiring-audit law

one compliance issue across 32 companies surveyed.

Italy fined OpenAI 15 million euro; a Rome court annulled it in March 2026 on jurisdiction, without examining the substance. Italy fined Clearview AI 20 million euro, never collected. The UK fined Clearview 7.55 million pounds in 2022, still unadjudicated on the merits four years later. New York City's hiring-audit law turned up one compliance issue across 32 companies surveyed. Annulled, uncollected, undecided, barely detected. Plan against the pattern in 4.1, not against the headlines.

“

Air Canada suggests the chatbot is a separate legal entity that is responsible for its own actions. This is a remarkable submission.

British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal · Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149

Air Canada's chatbot gave a passenger the wrong advice on bereavement fares. The airline argued that the chatbot was a separate legal entity, responsible for its own actions. The tribunal called that a remarkable submission. It awarded 812 Canadian dollars. The sum is small. The principle is not.

THE COST WITHOUT A REGULATOR

Two failures. No regulator involved.

Air Canada

wrong information
812 Canadian dollars

Zillow

304 million United States dollars in a single quarter
cut roughly 25% of its staff.

It is just never the whole question.
Air Canada's chatbot gave a passenger the wrong advice on bereavement fares. The airline argued that the chatbot was "a separate legal entity that is responsible for its own actions." The tribunal called that "a remarkable submission." It awarded 812 Canadian dollars. The sum is small. The principle is not. Zillow's home-pricing model was confidently wrong. The company wrote down 304 million United States dollars in a single quarter and cut roughly 25% of its staff. No regulator was involved. Accuracy is not irrelevant. Zillow was a forecasting failure and Air Canada was wrong information. It is just never the whole question.

QUIZ

Which change addresses the governance gap?

A rider-management algorithm assigns shifts. An audit shows it is accurate and well calibrated. Suspended riders receive an automated message. They can appeal, and the appeal re-runs the same algorithm.

A
Improve the model's accuracy further.

Accuracy was not the finding in the Italian rider cases. A well-calibrated model that cannot be contested still fails.

B
Publish a fuller explanation of how the algorithm works.

Explanation helps, and it is not what was missing. The finding turned on the absence of any route to contest. An explanation a rider cannot act on is not a route.

C
Give a person the authority to overturn the decision.

Foodinho's riders got “an automatic message without any possibility of providing explanations or contesting the decision.” An appeal that re-runs the same algorithm is not a review.

THE SECTOR LAYER

Singapore finance: advisory, and still unissued.

FEAT

MAS published FEAT in 2018: fourteen principles on fairness, ethics, accountability and transparency. It is advisory.

Guidelines on AI Risk Management

As at September 2026 they have not been issued, so the transition has not started.

Everything so far applies whatever business you are in. Your sector adds to it. In Singapore, MAS published FEAT in 2018: fourteen principles on fairness, ethics, accountability and transparency. It is advisory. MAS files it as an Information Paper, which its own hierarchy does not list as a regulatory instrument at all. MAS consulted on Guidelines on AI Risk Management in November 2025 and proposed a twelve-month transition after issuance. As at September 2026 they have not been issued, so the transition has not started.

“

Enough regulatory bite that we don’t need to write new rules for AI.

FCA Chief Data, Information and Intelligence Officer · Treasury Committee, 20 January 2026

The FCA was asked whether it would write AI rules. It said no. Its Chief Data, Information and Intelligence Officer told the Treasury Committee in January 2026 that the Senior Managers regime and the Consumer Duty together give the regulator enough regulatory bite that they do not need to write new rules for AI.

THE UK

Responsibility follows the activity.

The FCA

“enough regulatory bite that we don't need to write new rules for AI.”

technology systems

Chief Operations function

risk controls

Chief Risk function

The FCA was asked whether it would write AI rules. It said no. Its Chief Data, Information and Intelligence Officer told the Treasury Committee in January 2026 that the Senior Managers regime and the Consumer Duty together give the regulator "enough regulatory bite that we don't need to write new rules for AI." So who owns AI risk in a UK regulated firm? Somebody already does. Responsibility follows the activity, business area or function: technology systems normally sit with the Chief Operations function, risk controls with the Chief Risk function. The FCA considered creating a dedicated AI Senior Manager and decided against it, on the basis that existing governance already reached the problem.

WHAT TRAVELS BEYOND FINANCE

If nobody can be named, that is your finding.

Your sector regulator

probably already has a view

If nobody in your organisation can be named

that is a finding about your organisation rather than about the regulation.

Your sector regulator probably already has a view, and it probably is not written in a document with "AI" in the title. And the absence of an AI-specific rule does not create an absence of an owner. If nobody in your organisation can be named, that is a finding about your organisation rather than about the regulation.

QUIZ

Who must own this before launch?

A bank is launching a credit-decisioning tool built by a vendor. The business sponsor says the vendor is accountable for model performance. The risk function says nobody has asked it to review anything.

A
The vendor. It built the model and monitors it.

FEAT Principle 8: firms are “accountable for both internally developed and externally sourced AIDA models.” Outsourcing the build does not outsource the accountability.

B
A named senior manager inside the bank, with the risk function's review done.

Responsibility follows the activity and the function. The FCA declined to create an AI-specific role precisely because an existing owner already holds it.

C
Nobody yet. No AI-specific rule requires an owner before launch.

The absence of an AI rule is not an absence of an owner. FEAT, the Senior Managers regime and the Consumer Duty all attach to the firm regardless.

THREE QUESTIONS

Three questions for any AI proposal.

Accountability

Who is accountable when this is wrong, and what is their name?

Contestability

How does a person affected by this contest what it decided?

Disclosure

What have we told customers this does?

Few executives have time to assess every AI proposal properly. Most have time for three questions. Who is accountable when this is wrong, and what is their name? How does a person affected by this contest what it decided? What have we told customers this does?

WHERE EACH ONE COMES FROM

Each one comes from a case with consequences.

Accountability

FEAT Principle 8

Externally sourced models as well as their own.

Contestability

The Dutch, Deliveroo and Foodinho findings

Whether a person could argue with a decision.

Disclosure

Air Canada

The first AI-washing settlements brought by the SEC in 2024.

Each comes from a case you just saw. Accountability: FEAT Principle 8 makes firms accountable for externally sourced models as well as their own. A third of AI use cases in UK financial services arrive through third parties. Contestability: the Dutch, Deliveroo and Foodinho findings all turned on whether a person could argue with a decision. Disclosure comes from Air Canada, and from the first AI-washing settlements brought by the SEC in 2024. Two advisers paid 400,000 United States dollars between them for claiming to use AI that they were not using. One caution on the third. A New York regulator reviewed roughly 400,000 Apple Card applications. It found no discrimination by Goldman Sachs or Apple, and both could explain every complainant's decision when asked. The public criticism continued anyway. Being able to explain a decision will protect a firm in a regulator's assessment. On its own, it will not protect its reputation.

THE QUESTION THAT ACTUALLY DECIDES

What evidence would justify approving this, restricting it, or stopping it?

Tested

In the setting where it will run.

A person can intervene

Has the authority to overrule it.

Monitoring

Would show if it had drifted.

A stop or rollback exists

Somebody has actually tried.

Singapore's agentic AI framework

Systems “should not allow high stakes or irreversible actions to take place without human review.”

A firm can obtain satisfactory answers to all three and still approve a system with no evidence that it works. A fourth question closes that gap. What evidence would justify approving this, restricting it, or stopping it? Four things make up that evidence. It has been tested in the setting where it will run, not on the vendor's benchmark. A person can intervene, and has the authority to overrule it. Monitoring would show if it had drifted. And a stop or rollback exists that somebody has actually tried.

“

Systems should not allow high stakes or irreversible actions to take place without human review.

IMDA · Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI

Singapore's agentic AI framework states the hard line. Systems should not allow high stakes or irreversible actions to take place without human review. It does not prohibit autonomy. It prohibits autonomy where the action cannot be undone.

BACK TO THE CHATBOT

Back to the chatbot.

Whose name is on this?

How does a customer dispute what it told them?

What does your marketing claim it can do?

What happens when it is confidently wrong at two in the morning on a Saturday?

Return to the decision put to you 25 minutes ago. The supplier follows a voluntary framework. That answers none of the four questions. Ask these instead. Whose name is on this? How does a customer dispute what it told them? What does your marketing claim it can do? And what happens when it is confidently wrong at two in the morning on a Saturday?

QUIZ

Approve, restrict, or stop?

An AI tool flags insurance claims for manual review. It has a named accountable owner, a published appeals process, and accurate marketing copy.

It has been tested on the vendor's benchmark dataset. There is no monitoring in production and no rollback plan.

A
Approve. Accountability, contestability and disclosure are all in place.

Those three are necessary and not sufficient. None of them tells you whether it works in your setting.

B
Restrict. A limited pilot with monitoring and a rollback, then reassess.

The gap is evidence, not governance paperwork. A bounded pilot produces what a vendor benchmark cannot.

C
Stop. It cannot be deployed without production monitoring.

Defensible, and disproportionate here. The action is a flag for human review, which is neither high-stakes nor irreversible. Reserve stopping for decisions that are.

“

From the perspective of accountability and disclosure of policies and practices, HSBC had acquitted itself.

Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection · Re HSBC Bank (Singapore) [2021] SGPDPC 3

One case in this course ended well for the company. In 2021 a rejected credit-card applicant asked HSBC Singapore for the algorithmically generated scores behind the refusal. HSBC declined. Singapore's Deputy Commissioner agreed that the bank was entitled to decline, because the scores were evaluative opinion data. The law settled that. Then he went further than he needed to. He said that HSBC had acted reasonably by providing information about how it uses data and technology to conduct credit facility assessments, and that from the perspective of accountability and disclosure of policies and practices, HSBC had acquitted itself.

WHAT HE WAS POINTING AT

Two documents, published in advance.

A Principle for the Ethical Use of Big Data and AI

Published by HSBC before the complaint was made.

A Credit Decisioning Policy Statement

How data and technology are used to assess credit.

The publications did not win the case. They let a regulator satisfy itself quickly that the organisation was in control.
He was pointing at two documents that HSBC had published: a Principle for the Ethical Use of Big Data and AI, and a Credit Decisioning Policy Statement. The publications did not win the case. What they did was let a regulator satisfy itself quickly that the organisation was in control. It is the cheapest item on the roadmap that follows, and the only one with a regulator's endorsement attached.

YOUR ROADMAP

Start here. Then these three.

Weeks 0–3 · gate

AI inventory

Every AI use, including what people are already using without asking.

MAS P017-2025 §3.4

Designate an ownerA person for each consequential use. Not a committee, not the vendor.
Build a contest pathA route to a human with authority to overturn the outcome.
Put AI terms in procurementA third of use cases arrive through suppliers, and you are accountable for those too.
Beyond · triggered, not scheduled
  • ISO/IEC 42001 certificationwhen a contract or tender requires it
  • Assurance toolingwhen tracking by hand stops working
  • A dedicated AI functionwhen ad-hoc ownership stops scaling
This is the whole roadmap on one page. The inventory is a gate, not the first of four equal items: you cannot designate an owner for a use you have not listed, and you cannot build a route of appeal for a decision you have not found. MAS puts it at section 3.4 of the draft Guidelines. Once you have the inventory, the next three run in parallel. Designate an owner for each consequential use — a person, not a committee, and not the vendor. Build a route by which someone affected can reach a human with the authority to overturn the outcome. And put AI terms into your procurement, because a third of use cases arrive through suppliers and you remain accountable for those. On the right are the things that can wait. Notice they have no dates. Each one is triggered by a condition, because a date on a slide ages badly and a condition stays true. Certification when a contract or a tender scores it. Tooling when tracking by hand stops working. A dedicated function when ad-hoc ownership stops scaling. Screenshot this page. It is the only slide you need to keep.

FOR YOUR HIGHEST-CONSEQUENCE USE

Five fields. If you cannot fill them, that is the finding.

Use case
Automated triage of customer complaints
Accountable owner
Head of Customer Operations, by name. Not the vendor.
Contest path
None today. Escalated complaints are never re-read by a person.
Evidence it works here
Vendor benchmark only. Never tested on our complaint mix.
Next decision, and by when
Restrict to a pilot, by the end of this month.
A list of four good intentions is not a plan. Pick your highest-consequence use and fill in five fields. The use case. The accountable owner, by name. What a person affected can do about it. What evidence says it works here. And the next decision, with a date. Here is one worked through. Automated triage of customer complaints. The owner is the Head of Customer Operations, named, not the vendor. The contest path is none today, because complaints escalated by the tool are never re-read by a person before closure. The evidence is a vendor benchmark only; it has never been tested on our own complaint mix. And the next decision is whether to restrict it to a pilot, by the end of this month. That record took four lines and produced two findings and a deadline. Do it for your top three uses and you have the foundation of your governance programme.

CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING

What comes first?

A firm finished its AI inventory last month: 31 use cases, with named owners for the 6 it considers consequential. Next week it switches on a tool that automatically declines low-value insurance claims. No appeals route has been designed and there is no monitoring. The board has asked about ISO 42001 certification.

A
Start ISO 42001 certification. It answers the board and reassures customers.

Certification is usually secondary to closing a live control gap, and it takes months. The deployment is next week.

B
Design the appeals route and the monitoring before the tool goes live.

An automatic decline affecting customers with no route to contest is the pattern behind the Dutch, Deliveroo and Foodinho findings.

C
Extend the inventory to name owners for all 31 use cases.

Worth doing, and not what is about to go wrong next week. The inventory has already surfaced the thing that needs attention.
